headline: OpenAI's next GPT used 10,000 autonomous agents to crack a Millennium Prize Problem
summary: OpenAI's upcoming GPT model reportedly solved the Navier–Stokes equations, a Millennium Prize Problem, using a swarm of 10,000 AI agents working autonomously for 88 hours.
details: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman revealed that their next-generation GPT model, which recently proved the Navier–Stokes equations, will ship "soon." This breakthrough was achieved by a swarm of 10,000 AI agents.
These agents worked autonomously for 88 straight hours to produce a mathematical proof, then spent another 17 hours formalizing it into a machine-checked Lean proof, without human command.

The system's orchestration was unique: instead of a central controller, each of the 10,000 agents independently picked directions, shared progress, and borrowed ideas in real time. This contrasts with most multi-agent systems today.

Beyond Navier–Stokes, Altman claimed the same capability touched Riemann, Hodge, and the Kakeya conjecture, overturned the exponential time hypothesis, and produced a proof of Yang–Mills existence. The effort generated 722 research manuscripts.

Altman reportedly stated that "AI is now, most of the time, smarter than top scientists" and described the model as "only a few months old." While ambitious, such claims have preceded real releases from OpenAI.

This demonstration of autonomous, self-organizing research by agent swarms running for days without human direction signals a significant shift in the pace of discovery. The actual proof, however, still awaits external scrutiny.

headline_marked: Ukraine's new [[pocket-sized gadget turns Russian drones' cameras]] against them
headline: Ukraine's new pocket-sized gadget turns Russian drones' cameras against them
summary: The D·Vision SDR, a 10-ounce receiver from Kyiv startup CODE380, intercepts live, unscrambled video from many Russian drones, including newer Molniya models.
details: Ukrainian drone teams are using a new pocket-sized receiver, the D·Vision SDR, developed by Kyiv startup CODE380. This device picks up live camera video from many Russian drones and displays it on a screen. It weighs about 10 ounces, less than half the weight of some competing Ukrainian models.

Russian drones transmit their video over the air without scrambling, allowing anyone with the correct receiver to view the feed. This enables Ukrainian units to identify a drone's trajectory and target before it strikes.

The D·Vision SDR is also capable of listening to radio channels used by Russia’s newer Molniya drones for video transmissions, which began in June. Many existing detectors struggle to pick up these specific frequencies, giving the D·Vision SDR a crucial advantage.

However, Serhii “Flash” Beskrestnov, a radio specialist advising Ukraine’s president, has cautioned against over-reliance on such detectors. He warned that digital video could eventually replace analog, rendering current receivers ineffective.

Further challenges include reports from The New York Times in August that some Molniya drones are now AI-guided, utilizing Nvidia chips. These advanced drones emit no signals, making them undetectable by current signal-intercepting devices.
